analysis.one_liner: Requires every new car to test the driver's breath and refuse to start if they're legally drunk.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote; it sat in a House subcommittee from January 2019 until the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ordered the Department of Transportation to write a safety rule requiring every motor vehicle to carry an ignition interlock — a device that measures the driver's blood alcohol level and stops the car from starting if the driver is legally drunk. This targets drunk driving, which kills thousands of people on American roads each year. The bill was introduced by Rep. Debbie Dingell, sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, passed down to a subcommittee, and never received any vote before the two-year Congress expired.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who rides in or near a car: passengers, pedestrians, cyclists, and the families of the roughly 10,000 people killed in drunk driving crashes annually. Sober drivers benefit indirectly because impaired drivers could no longer simply get behind the wheel. Families who have lost relatives to impaired drivers, whom the bill's name honors, would gain a guarantee that new vehicles block a drunk driver from starting the engine.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers, passengers, pedestrians, and crash victims' families

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Department of Transportation to issue, within one year, a safety standard requiring every motor vehicle to be equipped with a device that measures the driver's blood alcohol concentration.
The device must prevent the vehicle from being operated whenever the driver's measured blood alcohol concentration reaches the legal intoxication threshold set in federal drunk-driving law.

Because the requirement applies to all motor vehicles, a drunk driver could not borrow a sober friend's car or use their own vehicle to get around an interlock order imposed only after a conviction — the protection travels with every car, not with every sentence.

analysis.who_pays: Automakers would bear the cost of engineering, installing, and maintaining a breath-testing interlock in every vehicle they sell, a cost likely passed to all car buyers. Vehicle owners would face a new device that must work correctly on every start — a false positive strands a sober driver. Privacy-minded drivers would be asked to submit to a breath test in their own car. Drivers who never drink-and-drive pay for protection against those who do.

drawbacks.text: The mandate applies to every motor vehicle, not just new cars produced after a phase-in, and gave the Department of Transportation only one year to write the standard — an unusually tight deadline for a change affecting the entire vehicle fleet.
Every car buyer pays for hardware that most drivers would never need to stop them, since the device guards against conduct by a small minority of drivers.

A device that must approve every engine start can misread a sober driver and leave them stranded, and requiring a breath sample in every car raises practical and privacy questions the bill does not address.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and concrete: technology that physically prevents a legally drunk person from starting a car addresses one of the leading causes of road deaths. The cost is real but routine for auto safety — automakers absorb compliance costs all the time, and the one-year deadline in this bill was aggressive compared to the multi-year phase-ins regulators usually get. The main design weakness is that the bill is a single blunt mandate with no phase-in schedule or false-positive standard; those details were left to the Department of Transportation. On balance, the public benefit outweighs the compliance cost, but the bill as written would have needed technical refinement in committee.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee for two years, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Debbie Dingell introduced the Abbas Stop Drunk Driving Act on January 11, 2019.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, the committee that handles vehicle safety standards.
On January 25, 2019, it was referred to the subcommittee on Consumer Protection and Commerce, and no further action was taken for the rest of the Congress.
The bill attracted no cosponsors at any point in the 116th Congress.
The bill never received a markup, a floor vote, or any vote in either chamber before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers are better off: they never had to add a blood-alcohol interlock to their vehicles, and buyers avoided the added hardware cost. The families of drunk-driving victims and everyone who shares the road got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Automakers, which never faced the mandate

for.name: Debbie Dingell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and named it for a drunk-driving victim; it received no cosponsors and she could not get it a committee hearing.

for.name: Department of Transportation
for.what_they_did: Would have been ordered to write the interlock safety standard within one year of enactment; the bill never passed, so no rule was ordered.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over motor vehicle safety standards
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 11, 2019 and never reported the bill out or scheduled a markup; it instead went to a subcommittee, where it remained for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Subcommittee on Consumer Protection and Commerce
against.role: Subcommittee of House Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 25, 2019 and took no further action on the bill for two years, until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got a vote, and with zero cosponsors even in a House controlled by the sponsor's own party, there is no roll-call record to show how support split by party.

industries.note: The bill would force every manufacturer to engineer and install a blood-alcohol interlock in every vehicle sold, a compliance cost passed to buyers. Because the industry's gain in this bill's outcome was avoiding the mandate, its interest ran against the safety rule that protects the public.

The bill would convert these companies' courtroom-ordered product into standard equipment in every new vehicle, a vast new market. Their business depends on the devices working to stop impaired drivers, so their interest lines up with the public's.

industries.industry: Alcohol sellers and the hospitality industry
industries.note: An effective in-car barrier to drunk driving would reduce the occasions on which patrons drive after drinking, cutting alcohol sales tied to that behavior. Ordinary businesses that serve alcohol responsibly would be only lightly affected.
